text:
A mode of doubling the length of stroke of a piston-rod, or the throw of a crank. A pinion revolving on a spindle attached to the connecting-rod or pitman is in gear with a fixed rack. Another rack carried by a guide-rod above, and in gear with the opposite side of the pinion, is free to traverse backward and forward. Now, as the connecting-rod communicates to the pinion the full length of stroke, it would cause the top rack to traverse the same distance, if the bottom rack was alike movable; but as the latter is fixed, the pinion is made to rotate, and consequently the top rack travels double the distance.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 118
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 118; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_118.html.

text:
Reciprocating rectilinear motion of the bar carrying the oblong endless rack, produced by the uniform rotary motion of the pinion working alternately above and below the rack. The shaft of the pinion moves up and down in, and is guided by, the slotted bar.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 119
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 119; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_119.html.

text:
The internal rack, carried by the rectangular frame, is free to slide up and down within it for a certain distance, so that the pinion can gear with either side of the rack. Continuous circular motion of the pinion is made to produce reciprocating rectilinear motion of rectangular frame.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 139
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 139; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_139.html.

text:
Movement used for varying the length of the traversing guide-bar which, in silk machinery, guides the silk on to spools or bobbins. The spur-gear, turning freely on its center, is carried round by the larger circular disk, which turns on a fixed central stud, which has a pinion fast on its end. Upon the spur-gear is bolted a small crank, to which is jointed a connecting-rod attached to traversing guide-bar. On turning the disk, the spur-gear is made to rotate partly upon its center by means of the fixed pinion, and consequently brings crank nearer to center of disk. If the rotation of disk was continued, the spur-gear would make an entire revolution. During half a revolution the traverse would have been shortened a certain amount at every revolution of disk, according to the size of spur-gear; and during the other half it would have gradually lengthened in the same ratio.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 142
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 142; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_142.html.

text:
Circular motion into alternate rectilinear motion. Motion is transmitted through pulley at the left upon the worm-shaft. Worm slides upon shaft, but is made to turn with it by means of a groove cut in shaft, and a key in hub of worm. Worm is carried by a small traversing-frame, which slides upon a horizontal bar of the fixed frame, and the traversing-frame also carries the toothed wheel into which the worm gears. One end of a connecting-rod is attached to fixed frame at the right and the other end to a wrist secured in toothed wheel. On turning worm-shaft, rotary motion is transmitted by worm to wheel, which, as it revolves, is forced by connecting-rod to make an alternating traverse motion.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 143
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 143; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_143.html.

text:
Continuous rotary motion of the disk produces reciprocating rectilinear motion of the yoke-bar, by means of the wrist or crank-pin on the disk working in the groove of the yoke.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 146
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 146; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_146.html.

text:
Circular motion into alternating rectilinear motion, by the action of the studs on the rotary disk upon one end of the bell-crank, the other end of which has attached to it a weighted cord passing over a pulley.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 154
provenance: Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements, 21st edition (1908), movement 154; public-domain excerpt. Transcription: https://507movements.com/mm_154.html.

text:
The two crank-shafts are parallel in direction, but not in line with each other. The revolution of either will communicate motion to the other with a varying velocity, for the wrist of one crank working in the slot of the other is continually changing its distance from the shaft of the latter.

— Henry T. Brown, Five Hundred and Seven Mechanical Movements (1908), no. 220
